findings.claim: Archetype glosses: 'fixes that fail — short-term reliability patches that mask architectural debt; limits to success — successful products hitting capacity ceilings; shifting the burden — outsourcing dependencies that erode in-house capability; tragedy of the commons — shared engineering capacity depleted...' (Ch 4)
findings.failure_mode: Archetype meanings imported from outside the source; the deep ref and source give the eight names only (Kim 2000)
findings.fix: strip the glosses, or re-cite the definitions to SSDL Brief 1.07 for the five it covers (fixes that fail, shifting the burden, drifting goals, success to the successful, limits to growth)

findings.claim: Maldives model: 'stocks (tourists, attractiveness), flows (arrival rate, departure rate), and feedback through pollution'
findings.failure_mode: Misdescribes the worked model: 'Attractiveness of the Maldives' is a factor computed from five inputs, not a stock; the described flow is 'Change in tourists', not arrival/departure rates
findings.fix: correct: stock (Tourists), flow (Change in tourists), and the factor 'Attractiveness of the Maldives' (from tourist numbers, crowding, bed supply/demand, prices, pollution awareness) feeding back on the flow

findings.claim: "Everything that has gone into the model is clearly visible in the network structure and probabilities. There are no 'hidden' decisions ..."
findings.failure_mode: Verbatim [V] passage carried without marker
findings.fix: re-mark: [V]

findings.claim: All eight archetypes glossed with software examples (e.g. 'escalation (competitor matches your engineering investment; both spend more, neither pulls ahead)'; 'growth and under-investment (product success outpaces engineering capacity until quality breaks)') cited to Ch 4
findings.failure_mode: Each example rests on an archetype definition the source does not give; cited to Ch 4 which lists names only; line 280 then says the distillation 'cites Barbrook-Johnson & Penn's presentation'
findings.fix: strip the glosses; keep the eight names; point to SSDL Brief 1.07 for template definitions

findings.claim: Core system engine = 'the central reinforcing or balancing loop'; example balancing loop 'technical-debt → defect-rate → engineering-time-on-fixes → feature-velocity'
findings.failure_mode: Engine is a set of central nodes/variables, not a loop; the 'balancing loop' example is an open chain (does not return to technical debt), so it is not a loop at all
findings.fix: correct: Build the CLD around a 'core system engine' (a handful of central variables) and the feedbacks among them; close the example (e.g. ... feature velocity → pressure to ship → new technical debt)

findings.claim: 'The reverse-engineering pattern surfaces missing intermediary steps that forward-only construction tends to gloss.'
findings.failure_mode: Rationale absent from deep ref and source, reads as the authors'
findings.fix: strip, or mark as the distillation's reading

findings.claim: Rich Pictures 'for stakeholder-communication of complex software-business situations' — 'designed for opening up exploration with stakeholders who might disengage from a CLD or ToC'; a non-technical board needs to 'feel' the tangle
findings.failure_mode: Recasts a participatory drawing exercise as a communication artefact. The source says Rich Pictures' value 'is often mostly in the process and discussions this generates rather than the picture itself as an output', and that analysing the pictures is hard; 'designed for stakeholders who might disengage' is not in the source
findings.fix: correct: Rich Pictures for having a mixed group (including non-technical board members) draw the situation together; the value is in the drawing and discussion, not the picture as a deliverable

findings.claim: "Be clear about whether you want value from the process, outputs, or both, of a mapping process."

findings.claim: Sequential combination 'one method feeds another, e.g., Rich Pictures → CLD → System Dynamics'

Sequential combination in Ch 11 means one method building on the outputs of the other. (Fig 11.2's specific combinations are not recoverable from the converted text.)
findings.evidence: Deep 89 ('cannot directly seed a CLD'), 293; source 1826-1836, 8398-8403
findings.fix: correct: e.g., CLD → System Dynamics (CLDs are 'a natural stepping-stone to simulation methods such as System Dynamics', Ch 4), with Rich Pictures used beforehand to open discussion rather than as an input

findings.claim: 'Outsourcing to a partner that erodes in-house capability over time is the [shifting-the-burden] archetype.'
findings.failure_mode: Applied question rests on an archetype definition absent from the source (names only)

findings.claim: 'Tactical AI deployment that masks underlying capability or process issues is the [fixes-that-fail] archetype.'
findings.failure_mode: Definition absent from the source; 'masking the underlying issue' is closer to shifting the burden (per SSDL's templates) than to fixes that fail (a fix whose side effects worsen the original problem)
findings.fix: correct: ...creating a fixes-that-fail pattern (a quick fix whose side effects make the original problem worse)? — cite SSDL Brief 1.07

findings.claim: Balancing loop example: 'technical debt → defect rate → engineering time on fixes → feature velocity, which constrains the reinforcing loop'
findings.failure_mode: Open chain labelled a balancing loop; misapplies the source's loop concept (B = self-stabilising feedback loop)
findings.fix: correct: close the loop or call it a chain that brakes the reinforcing loop

findings.claim: CLD session names 'fixes-that-fail ... quick patches that masked the architectural issue' and asks 'if we don't break the cycle this quarter, what does the model predict?
